title: Question 10
stem:
Carbon-15 ($^{15}_{6}\text{C}$) is an isotope of carbon that undergoes radioactive decay to nitrogen-15 ($^{15}_{7}\text{N}$), which is a stable isotope of nitrogen.

Radioactive decay is both a random and a spontaneous process.

parts.label: (a)(i)

markscheme_points.text: cannot predict when a (particular) nucleus will decay or cannot predict which nucleus will decay next

hints: Hint 1: Think about a large sample where you know the average rate, but zoom in on just one single carbon-15 nucleus - what can you say about when that one will decay?
parts.proper_answer: Random means it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, or which nucleus will decay next.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What random really means**
Think of yourself sitting beside a sample with millions of nuclei. You can predict the average behaviour very well, but for one named nucleus you have no clue. Random does not mean you do not know the half-life, it means the exact moment for that individual nucleus is fundamentally unpredictable.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A small sample of carbon-15 decays. The mass $M$ of carbon-15 in the sample decreases with time $t$.

Fig. 10.1 shows the variation with $t$ of the value of $\ln (M/10^{-16}\text{g})$.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

Fig. 10.1
parts.text: State how Fig. 10.1 demonstrates that radioactive decay is random.

markscheme_points.text: line fluctuates or trend is a straight line

hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the shape of the plotted curve in Fig. 10.1 - is it a perfectly smooth straight line, or does it wobble in small steps around an overall trend?
parts.proper_answer: The plotted line fluctuates about an overall straight-line trend, showing unpredictable short-term variations in decay rate.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reading randomness from the graph**
If decay were perfectly regular, $\ln(M/10^{-16}\text{g})$ against $t$ would be a perfectly smooth straight line. In Fig. 10.1 you see a jagged, stepped line that wobbles up and down around a straight trend. Those small irregular steps are the fingerprint of randomness - in short time intervals the number decaying fluctuates unpredictably.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: On Fig. 10.1, draw the straight line of best fit.

markscheme_points.text: straight line of best fit drawn on Fig. 10.1

hints: Hint 1: Think about how to average out the small random steps to show the underlying exponential law - where should a smooth straight line sit relative to the wiggles?
parts.proper_answer: A smooth straight line of best fit with equal scatter above and below, following the mean trend from about $\ln(M/10^{-16}\text{g}) = -4.8$ at $t=0$ to about $-8.0$ at $t \approx 11.6\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **How to draw the best fit**
You want to smooth out the randomness. Place your ruler so the straight line follows the middle of the jagged data, with roughly as many steps above as below along its whole length. It should start near $-4.8$ on the $\ln$ axis and fall steadily to about $-8.0$ at $t$ near $12\text{ s}$. Do not join dot-to-dot, draw one single straight line.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Show that the decay constant $\lambda$ of carbon-15 is given by the magnitude of the gradient of your line in (b)(ii).

markscheme_points.text: M = M0 exp (-λt) so ln M = ln M0 - λt so gradient = -λ (and magnitude of gradient = λ)

hints: Hint 1: Start from how mass decreases exponentially with time and think about what mathematical operation turns an exponential into a straight-line $y = mx + c$ form.
parts.proper_answer: Since $M = M_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$, then $\ln M = \ln M_{0} - \lambda t$, which is of form $y = c + mx$ with gradient $-\lambda$. Hence magnitude of gradient $= \lambda$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start from the exponential law**
Mass follows the same law as number of nuclei or activity because mass is proportional to number present:
$$M = M_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$$
where $M_{0}$ is the initial mass and $\lambda$ is the decay constant.

Step 2: **Take natural logs to linearise**
Take $\ln$ of both sides:
$$\ln M = \ln\left(M_{0}e^{-\lambda t}\right) = \ln M_{0} + \ln\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right)$$
$$\ln M = \ln M_{0} - \lambda t$$
This matches $y = c + mx$ with $y = \ln M$, $x = t$, intercept $\ln M_{0}$ and gradient $m = -\lambda$. So the magnitude of the gradient gives $\lambda$.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Use your line in (b)(ii) to determine $\lambda$. Give a unit with your answer.

markscheme_points.text: gradient = (-) (8.0 - 4.8) / (11.6 - 0) (allow any correct pair of values from Fig. 10.1)

hints: Hint 1: Pick two widely separated points that lie exactly on your best-fit line, not on the jagged data, and read off their $\ln$ values and $t$ values.
Hint 2: Divide the drop in $\ln$ value by the time interval to get the magnitude of the slope, and remember $t$ is in seconds so think about what unit $\lambda$ must have.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose a large triangle on your line**
Use your straight line, not the wiggly data. For example take $(t_{1}, y_{1}) = (0, -4.8)$ and $(t_{2}, y_{2}) = (11.6\text{ s}, -8.0)$ where $y = \ln(M/10^{-16}\text{g})$. A large $\Delta t$ reduces percentage uncertainty.

Step 2: **Calculate the magnitude of gradient**
$$|\text{gradient}| = \frac{|\Delta y|}{\Delta t} = \frac{8.0 - 4.8}{11.6 - 0}$$
$$|\text{gradient}| \approx \frac{3.2}{11.6} \approx 0.28$$
Since $|\text{gradient}| = \lambda$, then $\lambda \approx 0.28\text{ s}^{-1}$. The unit is $\text{s}^{-1}$ because $\lambda t$ must be dimensionless and $t$ is in $\text{s}$.

parts.label: (b)(v)
parts.text: Use your answer in (b)(iv) to calculate the half-life of carbon-15.
hints: Hint 1: Recall how half-life is linked to the decay constant through the time for the mass to fall to half its value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the half-life formula**
Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay. From $M = M_{0}e^{-\lambda t_{1/2}}$ with $M = M_{0}/2$ you get:
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$
$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.28\text{ s}^{-1}} \approx 2.5\text{ s}$$
This short half-life fits the rapid fall seen in Fig. 10.1.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The equation for the decay of carbon-15 can be written as

$$^{15}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{15}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\beta + ^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}.$$

State and explain how the mass of the products of the decay must compare with the mass of the carbon-15 nucleus.

markscheme_points.text: (for reaction to occur,) energy is released
energy release comes from fall in mass so total mass of products must be less (than mass of carbon-15)

hints: Hint 1: Think about whether a spontaneous nuclear decay can happen without giving out energy - what must be true about the total energy of the products?
Hint 2: Now link that released energy to mass using $E = mc^{2}$ and decide whether the products together must weigh more or less than the parent carbon-15 nucleus.
parts.proper_answer: Energy is released in the spontaneous decay, so from $E = \Delta m c^{2}$ this comes from a decrease in mass. Total mass of products ($^{15}$N + beta-particle + antineutrino) must be less than mass of $^{15}$C nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why energy must be released**
A spontaneous decay happens because the system can move to a lower energy state. Kinetic energy of the beta-particle and antineutrino plus any recoil must come from somewhere, so net energy is released.

Step 2: **Link energy release to mass**
By mass-energy equivalence $E = \Delta m c^{2}$, released energy appears as a loss of rest mass. Even though nucleon number 15 is conserved, the sum of the rest masses of $^{15}_{7}$N plus $^{0}_{-1}\beta$ plus $^{0}_{0}\bar{\nu}$ must be slightly less than the rest mass of the $^{15}_{6}$C nucleus. That mass difference $\Delta m$ provides the decay energy.
